interpretations: Count every inventory record per film rating (joined to film), find the average of the per-rating counts, and keep ratings whose count is strictly above that average. Return one row with the sum of those ratings' counts and the average of (count − average) across them, unrounded
Same as interpretation 1, but the "average of these counts" is computed over only ratings that have at least one inventory copy. Ratings with zero copies are excluded from the average
Same as interpretation 1, but the average includes all five ratings, even ones with zero copies
Count distinct inventory_id values per rating (the same as counting records, since inventory_id is the primary key)
Count distinct films per rating that have inventory, rather than copies
Count copies per rating separately for each store, then compare each store's rating count with that store's own average across ratings
Count copies per rating across both stores combined (the default reading), and compare each count with the overall average
"Above-average" means count ≥ the average rather than strictly greater than it. Under strict comparison, ties are excluded
The "average amount by which their counts exceed the average" is the mean of (count − average) over the above-average ratings only
The same quantity expressed as (sum of above-average counts / number of above-average ratings) − overall average. This is mathematically equal to interpretation
The average excess is taken over all ratings, with below-average ratings contributing zero
The average excess is taken over all ratings, with below-average ratings contributing their negative differences
The output is one row with two columns: total copies of above-average ratings, and average excess. The total could also be read as the sum of the excesses rather than of the counts
Ratings are taken from film.rating only. Films with NULL rating form their own group or are excluded
Inventory records whose film has no match are dropped (inner join). Alternatively they are kept as a NULL-rating group (left join from inventory)
Missing interpretations:
Count copies per rating by joining through film_category or other tables, which could duplicate copies, instead of the direct inventory-to-film join
Count only copies currently in stock (not out on an unreturned rental) rather than every inventory record
Count copies per rating using only one store's inventory, filtered to a single store
Compare each count with the median or the weighted average (total copies divided by number of films) rather than the simple mean of the per-rating counts
Report the average excess as an average of the above-average ratings' percentage excess, or as a ratio to the average, rather than an absolute difference
Return one row per above-average rating, instead of a single aggregated row
queries:
WITH c AS (
  SELECT f.rating, COUNT(*) AS cnt
  FROM inventory i
  JOIN film f ON f.film_id = i.film_id
  GROUP BY f.rating
),
a AS (
  SELECT AVG(cnt) AS avg_cnt FROM c
)
SELECT SUM(c.cnt) AS total_count, AVG(c.cnt - a.avg_cnt) AS avg_diff
FROM c, a
WHERE c.cnt > a.avg_cnt
SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT f.rating, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM inventory i JOIN film f ON f.film_id = i.film_id GROUP BY f.rating);
SELECT AVG(copies)
FROM (
  SELECT f.rating, COUNT(i.inventory_id) AS copies
  FROM film f
  LEFT JOIN inventory i ON i.film_id = f.film_id
  GROUP BY f.rating
);
SELECT f.rating, COUNT(DISTINCT i.inventory_id) FROM inventory i JOIN film f ON f.film_id = i.film_id GROUP BY f.rating
SELECT f.rating, COUNT(DISTINCT i.film_id) AS films
FROM film f
JOIN inventory i ON i.film_id = f.film_id
GROUP BY f.rating;
SELECT i.store_id, f.rating, COUNT(*) AS copies,
       AVG(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY i.store_id) AS store_avg_copies,
       COUNT(*) - AVG(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY i.store_id) AS diff_from_avg
FROM inventory i
JOIN film f ON f.film_id = i.film_id
GROUP BY i.store_id, f.rating;
